settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: normalize() does attempt to resolve '/./' and '/../' segments and returns null when '/../' is at index 0, indicating at least partial traversal handling.
getPathWithinApplication() strips the context path and is the documented, intended matching input, so the divergence window may be small on well-behaved containers.

PathMatchingFilter.preHandle() uses 'first match wins' over configured patterns and the request passes through untouched when no pattern matches; whether a bypass is reachable depends on the specific configured pattern set.
No index/control-flow evidence in this review proves an attacker-controlled URI reaches a filter-matching decision with a divergent normalized value.
candidates.description: Shiro's URL filter chain and authorization mappings match on WebUtils.getPathWithinApplication(request), which is derived from getRequestUri(). getRequestUri() takes the container-supplied request URI (or the javax.servlet.include.request_uri attribute), then calls decodeAndCleanUriString() and normalize(). decodeAndCleanUriString() URL-decodes once (using the request's character encoding, defaulting to ISO-8859-1) and truncates the string at the FIRST ';' character. normalize() then performs naive string surgery: replacing '\' with '/', collapsing '//', removing '/./', and resolving '/../' (returning null only when '/../' occurs at index 0). Crucially the method's own JavaDoc states it 'does not try to perform security checks for malicious input' and is 'useful only for normalizing application-generated paths.' Because this normalization can produce a path that differs from the path the servlet container actually used to select the servlet/dispatch, the value Shiro uses to choose which configured URL filters (authc, roles, perms, ssl, etc.) apply can diverge from the resource that is ultimately served. This is a classic path-confusion / access-control-filter-bypass precondition. Secondary risk: the single-pass decode does not handle double-encoded sequences (e.g. %252e%252e), and the truncation at the first ';' can interact with container path-parameter handling; these are container-dependent. Evidence: web/src/main/java/org/apache/shiro/web/util/WebUtils.java lines 110-121 (getPathWithinApplication), 135-141 (getRequestUri), 154-221 (normalize, incl. the WARNING JavaDoc and the index==0 '/../' check), 231-235 (decodeAndCleanUriString), and web/src/main/java/org/apache/shiro/web/filter/PathMatchingFilter.java lines 102-104 and 121-125 showing the normalized path is the value used for access-control path matching.
missing_evidence: No runtime tests or container-behavior verification (e.g. Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow normalization) were performed; divergence is inferred, not demonstrated.
No evidence of a concrete configured filter pattern that is bypassable, and no end-to-end data-flow proof from an HTTP request to an incorrect authorization decision.
Semantic resolution is reported as not_implemented, so call-site reachability of getPathWithinApplication was not computed.
No security test (e.g. WebUtils/PathMatchingFilter bypass test) was located in the web/src/test tree to confirm or refute the behavior.
preconditions: Application deploys Shiro's URL-based filter chain (IniShiroFilter / ShiroFilter / ShiroFilterFactoryBean) with authorization filters mapped to path patterns.
An attacker can craft a request URI whose Shiro-normalized form does not match a protected pattern but which the container still routes to the protected resource (or vice versa).
Container performs URI normalization/decoding differently from Shiro's single-pass normalize(), or the request uses include/forward attributes, backslashes, semicolons, or encoded dot-segments.
candidates.title: Path-based access control may be bypassable via request URI the container and Shiro normalize differently (WebUtils.getRequestUri/normalize)

counter_evidence: The key is randomly generated via AesCipherService.generateNewKey(), not a compiled-in constant, which mitigates the exact attack the JavaDoc warns about.
setCipherKey/setEncryptionCipherKey/setDecryptionCipherKey are provided so operators can supply a stable, secret key.
No evidence was found of a hardcoded key or of a weak/zero key being used.
candidates.description: AbstractRememberMeManager's class JavaDoc discusses a 'default encryption key' and warns that because Shiro is open source, anyone who knows the default key could reconstruct it and decrypt remembered identity data; it recommends configuring a custom key via setCipherKey. The constructor, however, does NOT use a hardcoded default key: it creates an AesCipherService and calls cipherService.generateNewKey().getEncoded(), so each instance gets a fresh random AES key at startup. This is primarily an observation about the security model rather than an exploitable flaw: behavior across restarts (remembered cookies surviving a restart require a stable, configured key) and multi-node deployments (each node generating a different key) are operational concerns. The candidate is reported only because the code and its own JavaDoc are in tension; no exploitable weakness is demonstrated here.
missing_evidence: No evidence of default-key usage being relied upon by any sample or test configuration was confirmed as a vulnerability.
No demonstration that a split key across instances leads to authentication bypass or data disclosure; this is operational/design, not a proven exploit.
preconditions: Application relies on RememberMe cookies and does not configure a stable cipher key via setCipherKey.
Multiple application instances or restarts occur such that the per-instance generated key differs between issuance and validation.
candidates.title: RememberMe cipher key is generated per-instance at construction rather than from a fixed default (AbstractRememberMeManager)
